Question #3): x <- 42 and y <- 42L look almost identical, but typeof(x) and typeof(y) give different answers. Explain the difference in your own words.

```{r}

typeof(x)
typeof(y)
```
Answer: The difference between x and y is the "L" in the number 42.

Question #5: When you ran the conversion-fail chunk, R produced NA and a warning instead of stopping with an error. Why do you think R is designed to give a warning here rather than crashing the whole script?

Ans. R only puts warning and doesn't crash because it makes line of codes by chunks, if one chunk had errors, it wont affect the other chunks.

Ans. both will produce true.

###Part D — Strings, paste(), and paste0()
Strings are stored as the character type. paste() joins strings with a space separator by default; paste0() joins them with no separator.

```{r}
# TODO: Print first_name and last_name using print() and/or cat()

first_name <- "Juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"

cat(first_name, last_name)

```
```{r}
# TODO: Use paste() to combine first_name and last_name into a full name
# TODO: Use paste0() to do the same, and compare the two results

paste(first_name, last_name)
paste0(first_name, last_name)
```
```{r}
# TODO: Use paste() with the argument sep = "-" to join first_name and
# last_name with a dash instead of a space

paste(first_name, last_name, sep="-")
```
```{r}
age <- 21

# TODO: Use paste0() to build the sentence:
# "Juan Dela Cruz is 21 years old." by combining full_name, age, and text

paste0(first_name, last_name, " is " ,age, " years old ")
```

###Conclusion
In 3–4 sentences, summarize what you learned about how R handles different data types, and why understanding typeof()/class() and conversion functions matters before doing arithmetic or combining data.

ans. R stores data using atomic vector types like logical, integer, double, and character, automatically coercing vectors to the most flexible type (such as converting numbers to text) when mixed values are combined. Function calls like typeof() reveal the underlying memory structure while class() identifies the high-level object behavior, making both essential for verifying how R interprets your data. Knowing these type distinctions—along with explicit conversion functions like as.numeric() or as.character()—prevents unexpected type coercion, subtle bugs, or calculation errors when combining datasets and performing arithmetic.
